pre.question: Why should the project boundary and intended Genie use case be explicit before the build starts?

options.label: So every later decision has a clear, governed target
So we can postpone scope until after implementation

coaching.governed_first: Correct — a clear boundary keeps the later semantic and agent decisions grounded.
coaching.prototype_first: Scope first is safer here; otherwise later outputs can drift away from the intended use case.

decision.question: Confirm the use case you'll build this Genie Agent for before continuing: proceed with the certified use case, or author your own custom use case first.

options.label: Proceed with the certified use case
Author your own custom use case first

coaching.use_certified: Confirmed — the certified use case is locked and this step can be completed.
coaching.author_own: Good override — draft your custom use case and lock it with vibe_set_parameters, then confirm to proceed.

post.question: Why lock a single use case before building anything else?

options.label: It anchors the PRD, semantic layer, agent, and dashboard to one governed target
So we can keep scope open and decide what to build later

coaching.anchor_everything: Correct — every downstream artifact reads back from the locked use case.
coaching.keep_open: The better answer is that it anchors everything — an open scope lets later steps drift.

post.question: What is the PRD's role for the rest of the workshop?

options.label: The context spine every later step reads from instead of re-interviewing you
A one-off document you can ignore once the build starts

coaching.context_spine: Correct — its personas, journeys, and entities ground every downstream decision.
coaching.throwaway_doc: The better answer is the context spine — measures, metric view, agent, and dashboard all read back from it.

post.question: Why analyze the silver-layer metadata before designing the gold layer?

options.label: To know the real tables, columns, and grain the gold model will be built from
It is optional; you can design gold from assumptions and fix it later

coaching.know_inputs: Correct — the gold design is only as sound as your understanding of the silver inputs.
coaching.skip_ahead: The better answer is to know your inputs first — designing gold from assumptions invites rework.

post.question: What is the gold layer optimized for?

options.label: Clean, business-ready tables shaped for analytics and the semantic layer
Storing raw, unprocessed source data exactly as ingested

coaching.business_consumption: Correct — gold is the business-ready layer the metric view and agent build on.
coaching.raw_ingest: The better answer is business consumption — raw, unprocessed data belongs in the bronze layer.

post.question: Why build the gold layer as a pipeline rather than a one-time query?

options.label: So the tables refresh repeatably and stay current as source data changes
A single manual run is enough; the data never needs refreshing

coaching.repeatable_refresh: Correct — a pipeline keeps gold current and reproducible as upstream data lands.
coaching.one_time: The better answer is repeatable refresh — a one-off query goes stale the moment source data changes.

post.question: Why deploy the lakehouse assets before building the semantic layer on top?

options.label: The metric view and agent need the governed tables to actually exist in Unity Catalog
Deployment is cosmetic; the semantic layer works against local drafts

coaching.real_tables: Correct — the semantic layer and agent bind to real UC objects, so they must exist first.
coaching.cosmetic: The better answer is that real tables must exist — the metric view can't reference a local draft.

decision.question: Which source strategy should we use for the semantic layer?

options.label: Reuse an existing governed source
Discover and qualify a new source

coaching.reuse_existing: Recommended — start with the governed source and expand only when coverage requires it.
coaching.discover_new: That is a valid override; record the qualification work before building on the source.

post.question: Why confirm your data source and bring in its context before designing measures?

options.label: The brief must be grounded in real tables, columns, and joins, not guesses
Design the measures first and find matching data afterward

coaching.ground_brief: Correct — locating real data keeps the brief and every later step honest.
coaching.design_first: The better answer is to ground the brief in real data first — measures without backing data can't ship.

post.question: What does profiling the schema verify before you commit to measures?

options.label: Which candidate measures the actual data — values, joins, coverage — can truly support
Only that the column names look presentable

coaching.data_supports: Correct — profiling separates measures the data can back from aspirational ones.
coaching.pretty_names: The better answer is what the data can support — profiling checks values, joins, and coverage, not cosmetics.

post.question: What makes a proposed measure useful to an agent and to the people reviewing its answers?

options.label: A named business meaning with a stable calculation
A raw column name without a defined meaning

coaching.business_metrics: Exactly — stable business meaning is what makes a measure reusable and reviewable.
coaching.raw_columns: Raw columns are inputs, not measures; define the business calculation and meaning first.

post.question: What does a metric view give a Genie agent that ad-hoc SQL does not?

options.label: Governed, reusable measures and dimensions with consistent definitions
Nothing but faster queries; the definitions are identical to ad-hoc SQL

coaching.governed_semantics: Correct — the metric view centralizes definitions so every answer stays consistent.
coaching.faster_only: The better answer is governed semantics — the point is one trusted definition, not just speed.

post.question: Why add synonyms to the semantic layer?

options.label: So the agent maps the words real users say to the right fields and measures
They are decorative and do not affect how the agent understands questions

coaching.map_language: Correct — synonyms bridge everyday phrasing to your governed field and measure names.
coaching.decoration: The better answer is mapping user language — synonyms directly improve how questions resolve.

post.question: What is the purpose of the agent description?

options.label: It tells the agent and users what it covers and who it serves, setting scope
It is just a display title with no effect on behavior

coaching.scope_and_audience: Correct — a clear description sets the agent's scope and audience expectations.
coaching.title_only: The better answer is scope and audience — the description shapes what the agent takes on.

post.question: What do good agent instructions primarily do?

options.label: Encode domain rules and guardrails that steer how the agent answers
Restate the table schema, which the agent already has

coaching.guardrails_behavior: Correct — instructions carry the domain rules and guardrails the schema alone can't express.
coaching.repeat_schema: The better answer is guardrails and behavior — repeating the schema adds little the agent doesn't know.

post.question: Why add verified queries to the agent?

options.label: They are trusted worked examples that steer the agent toward correct SQL patterns
They block users from asking anything else

coaching.worked_examples: Correct — verified queries anchor the agent to known-good SQL for common questions.
coaching.block_others: The better answer is worked examples — verified queries guide, they don't restrict what users can ask.

decision.question: Confirm that the benchmark answers are ready to load and verify the agent against.

options.label: Confirm and load the benchmark set
Not yet — keep the step open

coaching.confirm: Confirmed — the benchmark step can now be completed.
coaching.not_ready: No problem — keep refining the benchmark answers before confirming.

post.question: What are the benchmark questions used for?

options.label: To measure the agent's answer quality objectively and drive the optimize loop
As training data the agent memorizes verbatim

coaching.measure_quality: Correct — benchmarks give an objective score that the optimize loop works to raise.
coaching.training_data: The better answer is measuring quality — benchmarks evaluate the agent, they aren't memorized.

post.question: What does the optimize loop do with benchmark results?

options.label: Diagnoses failures and iterates instructions, metric view, and verified queries to raise the score
Nothing iterative — the first score is final

coaching.iterate_fixes: Correct — the loop turns failing benchmarks into targeted fixes, then re-scores.
coaching.one_shot: The better answer is to iterate — quality comes from measured loops, not a single pass.

post.question: Why build an AI/BI dashboard alongside the Genie agent?

options.label: It gives a governed visual surface over the same semantic layer for at-a-glance answers
It replaces the Genie agent entirely

coaching.complementary_surface: Correct — the dashboard and agent share one semantic layer and serve different question styles.
coaching.replaces_agent: The better answer is that it complements the agent — both read the same governed measures.

decision.question: Which activation scope should we plan first?

options.label: Activate the highest-value path now
Defer activation until more evidence is collected

coaching.activate_now: Recommended — start with the highest-value path and keep the scope intentionally narrow.
coaching.defer_activation: That override is reasonable when evidence or ownership is not ready yet.

post.question: What does 'activation' mean at this stage of the accelerator?

options.label: Putting the highest-value path into real use for its intended audience
Archiving the project so nobody can use it

coaching.put_to_work: Correct — activation is where the work reaches real users and delivers value.
coaching.archive: The better answer is putting it to work — activation is the opposite of shelving the project.

post.question: Why design synced tables for activation?

options.label: To serve the semantic-layer results to an operational app with low-latency reads
Only to make a backup copy of the data

coaching.serve_app: Correct — synced tables put governed data where an operational app can read it fast.
coaching.backup_only: The better answer is serving the app — synced tables are for live reads, not archival backups.

post.question: What does creating the synced tables accomplish?

options.label: It syncs governed UC data into Lakebase so an app can read it operationally
It deletes the source tables in Unity Catalog

coaching.uc_to_lakebase: Correct — the sync lands governed data in Lakebase for low-latency app access.
coaching.delete_source: The better answer is syncing UC into Lakebase — the source tables stay right where they are.

post.question: Why design the analytics app before building it?

options.label: To plan the audience, surfaces, and flows so the build serves the use case
Design is unnecessary; start coding and see what happens

coaching.plan_ux: Correct — a quick design keeps the build aligned to the audience and the use case.
coaching.skip_design: The better answer is to plan first — coding without a design tends to drift from the use case.

post.question: What are you doing when you build and wire the analytics app?

options.label: Connecting the UI to the governed data and the agent so users get real answers
Shipping a static mockup with no data connection

coaching.connect_data: Correct — wiring binds the UI to real governed data and the agent.
coaching.static_mock: The better answer is connecting the data — a static mockup can't answer real questions.

post.question: Why wire the app to Lakebase?

options.label: For fast operational reads of the synced, governed data from the app
To move the data into cold archival storage

coaching.operational_reads: Correct — Lakebase gives the app low-latency reads of the synced data.
coaching.cold_storage: The better answer is operational reads — Lakebase serves live app traffic, not cold archives.

post.question: What does wiring Genie into the app give users?

options.label: Natural-language questions answered in-app against the governed semantic layer
Only hard-coded charts with no natural-language ability

coaching.nl_in_app: Correct — wiring Genie lets users ask in natural language over the governed layer.
coaching.hardcoded_only: The better answer is natural language in-app — that is exactly what wiring Genie adds.

post.question: Why validate after deploying?

options.label: To confirm the deployed app and agent actually work end to end for real users
Deploying guarantees correctness; validation is unnecessary

coaching.confirm_works: Correct — validation proves the deployed experience works before users rely on it.
coaching.assume_ok: The better answer is to validate — a successful deploy doesn't guarantee correct behavior.

post.question: Why model the domain and its subdomains?

options.label: To give the agent a shared map of concepts and how they relate, improving routing and answers
It is documentation paperwork with no effect on the agent

coaching.shared_meaning: Correct — a domain model helps the agent interpret questions and route them well.
coaching.paperwork: The better answer is shared meaning — the ontology actively shapes how questions are understood.

post.question: What is the purpose of authoring ontology pages?

options.label: To capture concept context the agent uses to interpret questions correctly
To create marketing pages for external users

coaching.concept_context: Correct — pages carry the concept context that grounds the agent's understanding.
coaching.marketing: The better answer is concept context — ontology pages inform the agent, not external marketing.

post.question: What does the routing page do?

options.label: Directs incoming questions to the right domain or agent based on the ontology
Routes questions at random

coaching.direct_questions: Correct — the routing page sends each question to the domain best suited to answer it.
coaching.random: The better answer is directing questions — routing is deliberate, guided by the ontology.

post.question: Why is iterate-and-enhance an explicit step?

options.label: Real quality comes from measured iteration, not a single first pass
Once built, nothing should ever change

coaching.continuous_improve: Correct — iterating on real feedback is how the agent and app get genuinely good.
coaching.done_once: The better answer is continuous improvement — the first build is a starting point, not the finish.

post.question: Why redeploy and test after making changes?

options.label: To verify the changes actually work in the deployed environment users hit
Local edits are enough; deployed testing is redundant

coaching.verify_live: Correct — only a redeploy-and-test proves the change works where users actually run it.
coaching.local_enough: The better answer is to verify live — local edits can behave differently once deployed.

post.question: Why clean up the workspace at the end?

options.label: To remove orphaned resources that cost money or clutter the workspace
Never clean up; leftover resources are always harmless

coaching.avoid_cost_clutter: Correct — cleanup reclaims cost and keeps the workspace tidy for the next project.
coaching.never: The better answer is to clean up — orphaned resources can quietly accrue cost and clutter.
